purpose: Moving Regression creates a rolling smooth representation of chart data while allowing the trader to tune how closely the line follows recent curvature. It combines a local polynomial fit with a moving window, so its role is broader than a fixed moving average. The author proposes using the resulting curve to judge momentum and trend direction, identify possible reversals, and locate contextual support or resistance.
mechanism: Fit a polynomial of the selected degree to the specified prior-data window and evaluate the polynomial at the final data point to form each observation of the rolling line.
Optional direction coloring uses the fitted polynomial’s next-step direction: an upward projection produces green and the alternative produces red.
Longer windows and lower degree favor smoothing with lag; increasing degree can reduce lag while admitting more local noise. A constant-degree fit matches the same-window simple moving average.
outputs_and_use: Read the curve for trend confirmation, momentum and possible support/resistance; its short extrapolation is a directional suggestion rather than an independently validated forecast.
parameters: Length controls the moving fitting window; Local Polynomial Degree controls curvature. Predict Trend Direction enables the forecast-based coloring.
The author explicitly compares degree 0 with SMA, degree 1 with a linear fit, and degree 2 with a squared fit; no default length is disclosed.
risks: Analytical: high-degree fits can overreact to noisy windows and extrapolated direction can reverse as the window advances.
missing_information: Exact input price series, numerical fitting method, default length, and executable entry/exit rules are not specified.
data_reason: Historical chart prices support the described deterministic calculation class; algorithm parity remains unverified.

evidence.quote:
Moving Regression is a generalization of moving average and polynomial regression.

The procedure approximates a specified number of prior data points with a polynomial function of a user-defined degree. Then, polynomial interpolation of the last data point is used to construct a Moving Regression time series.
When the local polynomial is predicted to move up in the next time step, the color of the Moving Regression curve will be green.
When the degree of the local polynomial is set to 0 (i.e., fitting data to a constant level), the Moving Regression time series exactly matches the Simple Moving Average of the same length.

purpose: Nasan estimates a trade risk percentage and position size by combining the stock’s return relative to a benchmark, its historical volatility and drawdown, and the trader’s own performance assumptions. mechanism: Compute minimum and maximum risk from weighted annual stock-minus-benchmark returns divided by annual maximum and minimum ATR percentages respectively.

Blend transformed minimum and maximum risks using exponent and scaling factors derived from trader win rate and profit ratio. Aggressive and conservative modes exchange which factor receives the larger value.
Multiply the unadjusted risk score by a drawdown-tolerance adjustment, then combine capital, risk and a condition-dependent ATR multiplier to estimate size.
outputs_and_use: Use the estimated risk percentage and size to plan exposure; by default an underperforming stock receives no position-size calculation.

This script monitors each realtime update of the chart's feed. It first determines if price has moved up or down since the last update. The polarity of the price change, in turn, determines the polarity of the volume​​ and tick for that specific update. If price does not move between consecutive updates, then the last known polarity is used. Using this method, we can calculate a running volume​ delta and ticks delta for the bar, which becomes the bar's final​ delta values when the bar closes (you can inspect values of elapsed realtime bars in the Data Window or the indicator's values). Note that these values will all reset if the script re-executes because of a change in inputs or a chart refresh.

The indicator's core innovation lies in its logarithmic weighting system, where weights are calculated using the formula: [pine]w = 1.0 / math.pow(math.log(i + steepness), 2)[/pine] The steepness parameter controls how aggressively recent data is prioritized over historical data, creating a dynamic weight decay that can be fine-tuned for different trading styles. This logarithmic approach provides more nuanced weight distribution compared to exponential moving averages, offering better responsiveness while maintaining stability.

The LMA calculation combines multiple sophisticated components. First, it calculates the logarithmic weighted average of closing prices. Then it measures the slope of this average over a 10-period lookback: [pine]lmaSlope = (lma - lma[10]) / lma[10] * 100[/pine] The system also incorporates trend quality assessment using R-squared correlation analysis of log-transformed prices, measuring how well the price data fits a linear trend model over the specified period.

purpose: Benchmark forecast errors, temporal dependence, stationarity and interval behavior for model or strategy research. The library evaluates caller-generated predictions and observations; it provides neither forecasts nor trading decisions.
mechanism: Point-error APIs offer absolute/squared/root errors, normalized and percentage variants, including target offsets. Interval RMSE uses the midpoint of each lower/upper bound pair.
Temporal diagnostics compute autocorrelation at selected lags and an ADF unit-root statistic with critical value and observation count.

Interval sharpness is average width; resolution is width deviation; coverage is the fraction of targets inside intervals. Pinball loss uses quantile-weighted asymmetric errors; the matrix mean selects the lower bound at or below the median quantile and upper bound above it.

Historical bars on TradingView charts contain OHLCV data only, which is insufficient to calculate volume​ delta on them with any level of precision. To mine more detailed information from those bars we look at [I]intrabars[/i], i.e., bars from a smaller timeframe (we call it the [i]intrabar timeframe[/i]) that are contained in one chart bar. If your chart Is running at 1D on a 24x7 market for example, most 1D chart bars will contain 24 underlying 1H bars in their dilation. On historical bars, this indicator looks at those intrabars to amass volume​ delta information. If the intrabar is up, its volume​ goes in the Buy bin, and inversely for the Sell bin. When price does not move on an intrabar, the polarity of the last known movement is used to determine in which bin its volume​ goes.
1 — [I]On Bar Balance[/i]: This is the only balance using instant values; it is simply the subtraction of the Sell volume​ from the Buy volume​ on the bar.
2 — [I]Average Balance[/i]: Calculates a distinct EMA for both the Buy and Sell volumes, and subtracts the Sell EMA from the Buy EMA.
